stories.event: Rava poured drinks for guests at his son's wedding; two Sages stood for him and two did not.
stories.turn: Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas failed to stand before him.
stories.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them, asking whether they alone were Sages.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks to the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood when he poured for them, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not. Rava grew angry and asked sarcastically whether only they were Sages and the others not.

stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand before him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the guest did not rise for him, and Rav Pappa was angered.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served drinks to the Sages at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and objected when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, prompting a dispute over whether the Nasi may serve them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests, and Rabbi Tzadok cited God Himself providing for all creatures, justifying Rabban Gamliel's service.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel stood serving drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Eliezer declined the cup, but Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Rabbi Eliezer protested that they should not sit while the Nasi served them. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served his guests, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself sets a table for every creature, so Rabban Gamliel may surely serve them.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rabbi Meyasha's family
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls tied in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without telling anyone whose they were.
stories.turn: Ownership of the pearls was disputed and brought before Rabbi Ami.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the claimant, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet at the house of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha died without leaving instructions about them. The case came to Rabbi Ami, who gave the pearls to the claimant, because he knew Rabbi Meyasha was not rich enough to own them and the claimant could identify them by a mark.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership came before Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the claimant because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who then died without saying anything about it. The parties came before Rav Nahman, who ruled the goblet belonged to the claimant, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant could describe it by a mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rabbi Abba.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba gave the silk to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: Someone left silk at the house of Rav Dimi, who died without instructions about it. Brought before Rabbi Abba, the claim was decided for the depositor, because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the depositor identified the silk by a mark.

stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to Toviya and then died.
stories.turn: A man named Toviya came forward to claim it, raising the question of whether he was the intended Toviya.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya has come and receives the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After he died, a Toviya arrived to claim it. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

stories.actor: A son sent by his father
stories.event: A father told his son to climb to the top of a building and fetch chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
stories.turn: On his way down he fell and died, despite performing two mitzvot promising long life.
stories.outcome: His death was taken as proof that the promised reward refers to the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and bring him chicks. The son climbed, sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling both honoring his father and the mitzva of the nest, both of which promise long life. On the way back he fell and died, which Rabbi Ya'akov took to show that the promised reward belongs to the World-to-Come.

stories.event: Elisha ben Avuya witnessed a disturbing sight that undermined his faith.
stories.turn: By one account he saw a son die after performing the mitzvot of the nest and honoring his father; by another he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator dragged by a pig.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dust, and went out and sinned.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef says Elisha ben Avuya would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did. Some say he saw a son die returning from performing the mitzva of the nest at his father's command. Others say he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, killed by the government, being dragged by a pig, and cried out that a mouth that produced pearls should lick dust; after that he went out and sinned.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
stories.event: A man grabbed dinars from another person, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed to him.
stories.turn: The validity of a betrothal made with stolen money was brought before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the owner is not presumed to have despaired of the money.
stories.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man snatched some coins from someone else, tossed them to her, and said she was betrothed to him. The man came to Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that the owner of stolen goods despairs, so the coins were not his and the betrothal had no effect.

stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: He came to Rava to ask whether the betrothal was valid.
stories.outcome: Rava asked who had given him permission, ruling the onions stolen and the betrothal invalid.
stories.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his landlord's field to betroth a woman. When he asked Rava about it, Rava asked him who had allowed him to take them, meaning they were stolen and the betrothal failed.

stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for its owner.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he did not use the better, sharp sediment, raising the question of whether the owner had consented.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the betrothal was not valid.
stories.summary: A brewer making date beer for someone betrothed a woman with some of the beer's sediment. The owner discovered him and asked why he had not used the better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether this showed consent, and Rava ruled that 'go to the better ones' indicates consent only regarding teruma, so the sediment was not his to use.

stories.actor: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak and Rabbi Zeira
stories.event: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak used to juggle three myrtle branches while dancing before brides.
stories.turn: Rabbi Zeira complained the old man was shaming the Sages, but at his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira conceded that the old man's branch (or folly, or method) had earned him this honor.
stories.summary: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak would dance before brides juggling three myrtle branches, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was embarrassing the Sages. When Rav Shmuel died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign granted to only one or two people in a generation. Rabbi Zeira then said that the old man's branch, or his folly, or his method, had served him well.

stories.event: King Agrippa, though not required to, rerouted his entourage to yield to a bride's wedding procession.
stories.turn: A king, who has precedence, chose to give way to a bride.
stories.outcome: The Sages praised him for it.
stories.summary: Although a king of Israel takes precedence over a wedding procession, King Agrippa stepped aside to let a bride pass. The Sages praised him for this.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son and his wife
stories.event: After his wedding the man went to study for twelve years.
stories.turn: On his return his wife had become infertile, and divorcing her or taking another wife would both bring disgrace.
stories.outcome: Her husband prayed for her and she was cured.
stories.summary: A newly married man went off to the study hall for twelve years, and when he came back his wife was infertile. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi worried that divorcing her would make people say she had waited for nothing, and marrying another would make one a wife and the other a mistress. So her husband prayed for her, and she was healed.

stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years.
stories.turn: On returning he could not find his home, followed a girl he realized was his daughter, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was restored to life.
stories.summary: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study without waiting for him and stayed twelve years. When he returned the streets had changed and he could not find his house, until he heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up, recognized him, and died of the shock; he protested to God and prayed, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years of study, Rabbi Hama went first to the local study hall and sent word home to avoid shocking his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him, and Rabbi Hama, not recognizing his own son Rabbi Oshaya, regretted his absence and later stood up for him at home.
stories.outcome: His wife pointed out that a father does not stand before his son, revealing the young man's identity.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied for twelve years and, not wanting to repeat ben Hakhinai's experience, went to the local study hall and sent a message home first. A young man sat before him and asked keen questions, and Rabbi Hama sadly thought he would have had such a son had he stayed. When he went home and the young man followed, Rabbi Hama rose for him, until his wife asked whether a father stands before his son: it was his son Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter secretly betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father expelled her and vowed she would get nothing from him.
stories.turn: Akiva studied for twenty-four years and returned with twenty-four thousand students; his wife came to him, and her father, not knowing who the great man was, came to have his vow annulled.
stories.outcome: Akiva honored his wife as the source of all their learning, and revealed himself to his father-in-law, who fell at his feet and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, whose daughter betrothed herself to him in secret on condition that he go and study; her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing of his. After twelve years Akiva returned with twelve thousand students, overheard his wife say she would gladly have him study twelve more, and went back for another twelve years. When he finally returned with twenty-four thousand students, she came in poor clothes and fell at his feet, and he told his students that all their Torah was hers. Her father, hoping a great man could annul his vow, came to him, said he would never have vowed had he thought Akiva would learn anything, learned that this was Akiva, fell at his feet and gave him half his wealth.

stories.event: A gentile walking with a Jew could not keep pace, so he reminded him of the Temple's destruction to slow him down.
stories.turn: The Jew sighed but kept walking fast, and the gentile asked why groaning had not broken him.
stories.outcome: The Jew explained that a familiar sorrow does not devastate as a new one does.
stories.summary: A Jew and a gentile were walking together, and the gentile, unable to keep up, mentioned the destruction of the Temple to make the Jew grieve and slow down. The Jew groaned but still outpaced him. When the gentile asked why the sigh had not weakened him, the Jew said a sorrow one is used to does not overwhelm, as a woman used to losing children does not panic.

stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu stood in a bathhouse supported by two slaves when it collapsed under him.
stories.turn: He grabbed a pillar.
stories.outcome: He climbed out and pulled both slaves up with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, leaning on two slaves, when the building collapsed beneath him. He caught hold of a pillar, climbed up, and lifted both slaves out with him.

stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan was climbing stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi when the stair gave way.
stories.turn: He went up and pulled them both up, so the Sages asked why he needed support at all.
stories.outcome: He answered that he was saving his strength for old age.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was going up a staircase with Rav Ami and Rav Asi supporting him when the stair collapsed. He climbed up and pulled both of them up after him. When the Sages asked why so strong a man needed support, he said that otherwise he would have nothing left for his old age.

stories.actor: Mari bar Isak and his claimed brother
stories.event: A man claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother came from Bei Hoza'a and demanded a share of their father's estate.
stories.turn: Mari denied knowing him, and the claimant said his witnesses were afraid of the violent Mari.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda placed the burden on Mari to prove the man was not his brother, telling him this is how he judges violent men.
stories.summary: A man arrived from Bei Hoza'a claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother and asked for a share of their father's property, but Mari said he did not know him. Rav Hisda first noted that brothers may fail to recognize each other, as Joseph's brothers did, and told the claimant to bring witnesses. When the claimant said his witnesses feared Mari, a violent man, Rav Hisda ordered Mari to bring witnesses that he was not his brother; when Mari protested that the claimant bears the burden of proof, Rav Hisda said this is how he judges him and all violent men.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, Rabbi Afes and Levi
stories.event: Appointed head of the yeshiva by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Hanina declined in favor of the older Rabbi Afes and sat outside, with Levi joining him.
stories.turn: Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the headship, and Levi, left without a study partner, went to Babylonia.
stories.outcome: When Rav heard that a great limping man had come to Neharde'a, he deduced the whole chain of events.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ordered that Hanina bar Hama head the yeshiva, but Rabbi Hanina refused because Rabbi Afes was two and a half years older; Rabbi Afes sat at the head while Rabbi Hanina sat outside, and Levi sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, and Levi, with no one to study with, went to Babylonia. Told that a great man who limped had arrived in Neharde'a and was teaching, Rav concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Levi had come.

stories.event: A year after losing money to honor his father, Dama ben Netina had a red heifer born in his herd.
stories.turn: The Sages of Israel came to buy it, ready to pay any price.
stories.outcome: He asked only for the amount he had lost honoring his father.
stories.summary: The next year God rewarded Dama ben Netina: a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he told them he knew they would pay any sum, but he asked only for the money he had lost for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among the nobles of Rome in a golden cloak.
stories.turn: His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina was once sitting among the Roman nobility wearing a golden cloak. His mother came, tore it from him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. He did not embarrass her in return.

stories.actor: Rav Hamnuna and the Elders of Nezonya
stories.event: The Elders of Nezonya stopped attending Rav Hisda's lecture, and Rav Hisda sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them.
stories.turn: They challenged Rav Hamnuna with a question about a castrated slave that he could not answer, and mocked his name.
stories.outcome: Rav Hamnuna reported to Rav Hisda, who told him the answer was in a baraita he should have known.
stories.summary: When the Elders of Nezonya stopped coming to his lecture, Rav Hisda sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. They told him they stayed away because Rav Hisda had not answered their question, and when Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him, they asked whether a slave castrated by his master goes free. He had no answer, and they mocked him by calling him Karnuna, a cold fish, instead of Hamnuna. He returned to Rav Hisda, who told him that the answer was in a baraita.

stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Ami that someone had presumptive status as a priest because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether he read first as a priest or as a prominent man, and the witness said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on that testimony.
stories.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami and said that someone was presumed a priest because he had been called to the Torah first. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was because he was a priest or because he was a great man. When the witness said a Levite had read after him, Rabbi Ami recognized the man as a priest.

stories.actor: A witness and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was presumed a Levite because he read second from the Torah.
stories.turn: Asked whether he read second as a Levite or for his prominence, the witness said a priest had read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the man to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was presumed a Levite because he was called second to the Torah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked whether that reflected his lineage or his stature, and the witness answered that a priest had read before him. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recognized him as a Levite.

stories.event: When a witness claimed priestly status for someone who read first from the Torah, Reish Lakish demanded evidence of receiving teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected.
stories.turn: Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same case arose and Rabbi Yohanan gave Rabbi Elazar's exact objection, revealing Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
stories.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah; Reish Lakish asked whether he had been seen receiving teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked whether priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. On another occasion, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, a similar case came up, Reish Lakish asked the same question, and Rabbi Yohanan gave the same reply. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and asked why he had not said the teaching in the name of bar Nappaha.

stories.event: A man mentioned offhandedly that as a child his father carried him from school, had him immersed, and let him eat teruma that evening.
stories.turn: He added that his friends kept away from him and nicknamed him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevated him to the priesthood on the basis of his statement.
stories.summary: A man speaking casually recalled being carried on his father's shoulder out of school as a boy, stripped and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening. As Rabbi Hiyya told it, he added that his friends kept their distance and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. On the strength of this offhand remark, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recognized him as a priest.

stories.event: Mar Ukva and his wife, secretly leaving charity at a poor man's door, were chased and hid in a still-hot furnace.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva's feet were burned while his wife's were not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: His wife explained that her charity, given as ready food at home, was more immediate than his.
stories.summary: When the poor man saw someone at his door, he came out after them, and Mar Ukva and his wife ran and hid in a furnace whose fire had been banked but was still hot. Mar Ukva's feet were burning, and his wife told him to rest them on hers. He was dismayed that she was spared, and she explained that she gives at home in food the poor can use at once, so her charity was greater.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his usual four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor on the eve of Yom Kippur by his son.
stories.turn: His son returned saying the man did not need it, since he saw old wine being sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva concluded the man was that pampered and doubled the gift.
stories.summary: Every Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor man nearby. One year his son brought the money back, reporting that the man did not need it because they were sprinkling old wine for him. Mar Ukva said that if he was used to such luxury, he needed more, and doubled the sum.

stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He judged it insufficient provision for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half his remaining fortune.
stories.summary: As he was dying, Mar Ukva asked to see his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the road was long, he rose and gave away half his wealth.

stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his usual four dinars to a poor man on Shabbat eve by his wife.
stories.turn: She returned saying the man did not need it, having overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina cited Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failings toward the truly poor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a certain poor man every Friday. One week his wife brought them back, saying she had heard the household ask him whether he ate on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina remarked that this is why Rabbi Elazar said we should be grateful to swindlers, for without them we would be sinning every day by neglecting the poor.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
stories.event: A widow was taking the orphans to court to claim her marriage contract.
stories.turn: The orphans, embarrassed by her house clothes, asked her to dress properly, so she put on all her garments.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled, following Rav, that the clothes on her are appraised and counted against her marriage contract.
stories.summary: The daughter-in-law of bar Elyashiv's family was suing the orphans for her marriage contract. The orphans said it shamed them for her to go to court dressed like that, so she put on all her clothes. Before Ravina, he ruled that a widow's clothes on her are valued and deducted, so everything she wore counted.

stories.event: A man instructed in his will that his daughter be given a dowry.
stories.turn: The cost of a dowry dropped before it was paid.
stories.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the saving goes to the male orphans.
stories.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a dowry, and then the price of dowries fell. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled that the difference belongs to the sons, not the daughter.

stories.event: A man instructed that his daughter receive four hundred dinars' worth of his wine.
stories.turn: The wine rose in value.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled the gain goes to the male orphans.
stories.summary: A man willed his daughter four hundred dinars of wine, and the wine then became more valuable. Rav Yosef ruled that the extra value belongs to the sons.

stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, troubled by their stepmother's wasteful spending, followed his advice to have their father set aside land for her sustenance.
stories.turn: After their father died, Reish Lakish ruled the land only added to her support and threatened them if they did not pay.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing, as an equal of his disagreed.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan had a stepmother who was squandering their father's money on her upkeep, and Rabbi Yohanan advised them to have their father designate land for her sustenance. After the father's death they went to Reish Lakish, who said the land only increased her support and threatened to make them forget Rabbi Yohanan if they did not pay her. When they complained to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could do nothing, since a man equal to him disagreed.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandchild to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
stories.turn: Asked why he rushed so, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse linking teaching grandchildren to standing at Sinai.
stories.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba once met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with only a cheap covering on his head. When he asked why all the haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered that the Torah juxtaposes teaching one's grandchildren with standing before God at Horeb. From then on, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never ate breakfast until he had reviewed with his child and added to his lesson.

stories.event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son cut it to six years, then insisted on marrying first; he studied twelve years afterward and returned to find his wife infertile.
stories.outcome: His father reassured him, and after the twelve years he prayed for his wife and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, agreeing he would study twelve years first. When the bride passed before him, the son asked for six years, and then said he would marry first and study later; he was ashamed before his father, who told him he had acted as God did in bringing forward the Sanctuary. After the wedding he studied twelve years, came back to find his wife infertile, and since divorce or a second wife would both bring disgrace, he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years.
stories.turn: Returning, he could not find his house, followed his daughter home, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she lived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast for the study hall without waiting for him and stayed twelve years. When he came back the paths of his town had changed, and he found his home only by following a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai'. His wife saw him, her heart fluttered and she died; he cried out to God and prayed, and she lived again.

stories.event: After twelve years of study Rabbi Hama went to the local study hall first and sent word home.
stories.turn: He did not recognize his brilliant son Rabbi Oshaya, lamented his absence, and stood for him when they went home.
stories.outcome: His wife asked whether a father stands before his son, revealing who he was.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returned after twelve years of study and, to avoid ben Hakhinai's mistake, went first to the local study hall and sent a message home. A sharp young man questioned him and he regretted that he had not stayed home to raise such a son. When they both entered his house he stood up for the young man, and his wife asked whether a father stands before his son: it was Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter betrothed herself privately to the shepherd Akiva on condition he study; her father expelled her and vowed to give her nothing.
stories.turn: Akiva studied twelve years and returned with twelve thousand students, overhearing an old man taunting his wife.
stories.outcome: The story continues past the window.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was Ben Kalba Savua's shepherd, and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter, seeing his modesty, betrothed herself to him in secret on condition he go to study. Her father threw her out and vowed she would not benefit from his property. Akiva studied twelve years and came back with twelve thousand students, and as he approached he heard an old man speaking to his wife.

stories.event: A never-married man claimed before Rav Nahman that he had found his bride not a virgin.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman reasoned that a bachelor could only know this from experience with prostitutes.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A man who had never been married told Rav Nahman that on his wedding night he found an unobstructed opening. Rav Nahman said that since he could only know this from visiting prostitutes, he should be flogged with palm branches.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
stories.event: A man grabbed dinars from someone, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed.
stories.turn: He brought the question of the betrothal before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the owner had not despaired of the money, so the betrothal was void.
stories.summary: While a woman was washing her feet, a man snatched coins from another person, threw them to her and said she was betrothed to him. When the case came to Rava, he ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim despairs, so the coins were not the man's and the betrothal was invalid.

stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from his landlord's field.
stories.turn: He asked Rava whether the betrothal held.
stories.outcome: Rava asked who had permitted him to take them, ruling them stolen and the betrothal invalid.
stories.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked. Rava asked him who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen and the betrothal failed.

stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for its owner.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he did not use the better sediment.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark indicates consent only for teruma, so the betrothal was not valid.
stories.summary: A brewer used beer sediment belonging to his employer to betroth a woman, and the owner, finding him, asked why he had not used the better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner consented. Rava ruled that 'go to the better ones' shows consent only in the case of teruma.

stories.event: Ravin went as an agent to betroth a woman for his son.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son.
stories.outcome: Ravin betrothed her to himself without first telling his son, fearing someone else would take her in the meantime.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman on behalf of his son, but betrothed her to himself instead. The Gemara explains that her family refused to give her to his son, and he did not go back to inform his son first because he feared another man would betroth her in the meantime.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him.
stories.turn: The land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana.
stories.outcome: Rav bought it for himself without first informing him, fearing another buyer would take it.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him, and Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara explains that the land lay among violent men who would deal with Rav but not with Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared that if he went back to tell him, someone else would buy it first.

stories.event: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it.
stories.turn: Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who complained to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival with the case of a pauper whose loaf is snatched.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba said he had not known, refused to sell his first land as a bad omen, and offered it to Rav Giddel as a gift.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was in the middle of buying a field when Rabbi Abba bought it instead. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, and he waited until Rabbi Abba came up for the Festival and asked him what is said of one who takes a loaf a poor man is reaching for. Rabbi Abba answered that he is called wicked, said he had not known about Rav Giddel, and, unwilling to sell the first land he ever bought, offered to give it to Rav Giddel as a gift.
